**What this script does.** It fits the regression models of the main text
and the intersectional model with four characteristics (M4), and estimates
the effect of ALE participation on literacy for each intersectional group.

| Output file (in `Results/`) | Paper |
|---|---|
| `Table_A2.docx/.csv` | Appendix Table A2 (OLS, M1.1–M1.4) |
| `Table_A3.docx/.csv` | Appendix Table A3 (multilevel, M2.1–M2.5) |
| `Table_A4.docx/.csv` | Appendix Table A4 (M4, four-way intersections) |
| `Fig_2.png`, `Fig_2_data.csv` | Figure 2 (effect of ALE by group, from M4) |
| `Table_weight_check.csv` | Weighted vs unweighted comparison (text on weights) |

**Input.** `Data/df2.RDS` from `01_Data_Setup.Rmd`.
**Output for 04.** `Data/models_03.rds` (the fitted models), so that 04
runs on its own.

**Analysis sample.** Adults not in formal education with valid values on
every model variable (`in_sample == 1` from 01).

**Country weights.** Every country has the same influence: each respondent
is weighted by (average sample size per country) / (own country's sample
size). Within a country every respondent counts the same, i.e. the PIAAC
survey weights are not used in the models (see the weighting check below).

**Literacy.** The outcome is the mean of the ten plausible values
(`skill_reading`).

**Effects of ALE by group.** For each group (e.g. foreign-born,
non-native-speaking mothers) the effect is the difference in predicted
literacy between ALE = 1 and ALE = 0 with the group's characteristics
fixed. The same model coefficients apply to every country, so each group
has one effect: a weighted sum of coefficients. Its standard error comes
directly from the covariance matrix of the coefficients. These are
conditional average treatment effects, one per group, i.e. heterogeneous
treatment effects across groups. The functions are in
`R/functions_models.R`.

## Setup

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(here)
source(here("R", "load_packages.R"))
source(here("R", "functions_models.R"))

packages <- c("tidyverse", "here", "knitr", "lme4", "performance",
              "flextable", "viridis", "patchwork", "ragg")
load_packages(packages)

dir.create(here("Results"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

### Settings

`random_slope = TRUE` lets the effect of ALE vary across countries (a
random slope for `NFE12_within`). The fixed ALE coefficients, and with
them the group effects, are then averages over countries, and their
standard errors include the variation between countries. Set it to
`FALSE` for random intercepts only.

```{r settings}
random_slope <- TRUE
random_part  <- if (random_slope) "(1 + NFE12_within | iso3c)" else "(1 | iso3c)"
random_part
```

## Data

```{r data}
df2 <- read_rds(here("Data", "df2.RDS"))
d   <- prep_model_data(df2)

cat(nrow(d), "respondents in", n_distinct(d$iso3c), "countries\n")

d %>%
  group_by(iso3c) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), weight = first(cweight),
            pct_foreign_born = 100 * mean(FORBORN)) %>%
  kable(digits = 2)
```

## Table A2. OLS with country fixed effects

M1.1 foreign-born only, M1.2 native-born only, M1.3 both, M1.4 both with an
ALE × foreign-born interaction. Country dummies absorb differences in
average literacy between countries; age group is a control.

```{r ols}
ols_rhs <- "NFE12 + female + children + FORLANG + tertiary + age_group + factor(iso3c)"

ols <- list(
  M1.1 = lm(as.formula(paste("skill_reading ~", ols_rhs)),
            data = filter(d, FORBORN == 1), weights = cweight),
  M1.2 = lm(as.formula(paste("skill_reading ~", ols_rhs)),
            data = filter(d, FORBORN == 0), weights = cweight),
  M1.3 = lm(as.formula(paste("skill_reading ~ FORBORN +", ols_rhs)),
            data = d, weights = cweight),
  M1.4 = lm(as.formula(paste("skill_reading ~ FORBORN * NFE12 +", ols_rhs)),
            data = d, weights = cweight))

table_a2 <- model_table(ols)
save_table(table_a2, "Table_A2",
           "Table A2. OLS regressions of literacy on ALE participation (country fixed effects, equal country weights)")
kable(table_a2)
```

### Weighting check

The models do not use the PIAAC survey weights. Following Rabe-Hesketh and
Skrondal (2006), this is justified when the variables the weights depend
on are in the model. PIAAC's weights are calibrated on age, sex,
education and region (and in some countries birth country); the models
include all of these except region. Two checks:

1. The correlation of M1.3's residuals with the survey weight, as in the
   draft (weights divided by each country's smallest weight).
2. M1.3 refitted with the survey weights (each country's weights rescaled
   to the same total, so countries still count equally). If the
   coefficients barely move, the weights carry little extra information.

```{r weight_check}
d_m13 <- d %>% mutate(resid = residuals(ols$M1.3))
cor.test(d_m13$aweight, d_m13$resid)

d_sw <- d %>% mutate(sweight = SPFWT0 / ave(SPFWT0, iso3c, FUN = sum) * 1000)
m13_sw <- lm(formula(ols$M1.3), data = d_sw, weights = sweight)

weight_check <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(ols$M1.3)),
  equal_country_weights = coef(ols$M1.3),
  survey_weights = coef(m13_sw)) %>%
  filter(!grepl("iso3c", term)) %>%
  mutate(difference = survey_weights - equal_country_weights)
write_csv(weight_check, here("Results", "Table_weight_check.csv"))
kable(weight_check, digits = 2)
```

## Table A3. Multilevel models with within- and between-country effects

Each characteristic enters twice: its country mean (between, z-scored
across countries) and the person's deviation from it (within).

- M2.1 foreign-born only, M2.2 native-born only (no foreign-born terms).
- M2.3 both, main effects. M2.3b adds GDP per capita (log, capped).
- M2.4 adds ALE × foreign-born (within).
- M2.5 adds ALE × each of sex, parenthood, foreign-born and language.

```{r m2}
stems_no_fb <- c("NFE12", "female", "children", "forlang", "ed3_tertiary")
stems_all   <- c(stems_no_fb, "forborn")

m2 <- list(
  M2.1  = fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_no_fb, random = random_part), filter(d, FORBORN == 1)),
  M2.2  = fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_no_fb, random = random_part), filter(d, FORBORN == 0)),
  M2.3  = fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_all, random = random_part), d),
  M2.3b = fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_all, extra = "gdppc_k_log", random = random_part), d),
  M2.4  = fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_all, extra = "NFE12_within:forborn_within",
                               random = random_part), d),
  M2.5  = fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_all,
                               extra = c("NFE12_within:female_within",
                                         "NFE12_within:children_within",
                                         "NFE12_within:forborn_within",
                                         "NFE12_within:forlang_within"),
                               random = random_part), d))

table_a3 <- model_table(m2)
save_table(table_a3, "Table_A3",
           "Table A3. Linear mixed models of literacy, within- and between-country effects (ML, equal country weights)")
kable(table_a3)
```

## Table A4. Four-way intersectional model (M4)

M2.3 plus the full interaction of the within parts of sex, foreign-born,
parenthood, language and ALE (all sub-interactions included).

```{r m4}
m4 <- fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_all,
                           interaction = c("female", "forborn", "children", "forlang", "NFE12"),
                           random = random_part), d)

table_a4 <- model_table(list(M4 = m4))
save_table(table_a4, "Table_A4",
           "Table A4. Linear mixed model with four-way intersections (M4)")
kable(table_a4)
VarCorr(m4)
```

## Figure 2. Effect of ALE by group (M4)

Bars are the effects with 95% confidence intervals.

```{r fig2}
fig2 <- profile_ates(m4, d)
write_csv(fig2 %>% mutate(type_label = gsub("\n", " ", type_label)),
          here("Results", "Fig_2_data.csv"))

save_png(plot_effects(fig2), "Fig_2.png")
include_graphics(here("Results", "Fig_2.png"))

fig2 %>% select(type_id, ATE, se, lower, upper) %>% kable(digits = 1)
```

### Checks on the effect estimates

1. The effect from the coefficients equals the average difference in
   predictions over the whole sample (the approach of the earlier code),
   and that difference is the same for every respondent.
2. Standard errors compared across approaches: this model, the same model
   with random intercepts only, and the earlier t-test on predicted
   values.

```{r ate_checks}
gm <- grand_means(d)
g1 <- list(female = 1, forborn = 1, children = 1, forlang = 1)
p0 <- predict(m4, newdata = set_group(d, g1, 0, gm), re.form = NA)
p1 <- predict(m4, newdata = set_group(d, g1, 1, gm), re.form = NA)
c(prediction_difference = mean(p1 - p0), from_coefficients = fig2$ATE[1],
  sd_of_difference_across_people = sd(p1 - p0))

m4_ri <- fit_lmm(make_formula(stems_all,
                              interaction = c("female", "forborn", "children", "forlang", "NFE12"),
                              random = "(1 | iso3c)"), d)
fig2_ri <- profile_ates(m4_ri, d)

tibble(type_id = fig2$type_id,
       ATE_random_slope = fig2$ATE, se_random_slope = fig2$se,
       ATE_random_intercept = fig2_ri$ATE, se_random_intercept = fig2_ri$se) %>%
  kable(digits = 2)

# what the earlier t-test reported as the standard error for group 1f
t.test(p1, p0)$stderr
```

The earlier t-test compared two columns of 126,000 predictions. Its
standard error reflects how much predicted literacy varies between people
and how many rows there are, not the uncertainty of the effect, so it is
not a valid standard error.
